claim: Mutations in human Atrophin1 cause dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, a neurodegenerative disease.
source: Mutations in human Atrophin1, a transcriptional corepressor, cause dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, a neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: Supported by citations to Koide et al., 1994 and Nagafuchi et al., 1994 in the Introduction section.

claim: Drosophila Atrophin mutants display neurodegeneration, segmentation, patterning and planar polarity defects.
source: Drosophila Atrophin (Atro) mutants display many phenotypes, including neurodegeneration, segmentation, patterning and planar polarity defects.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2002; Fanto et al., 2003; Charroux et al., 2006; Napoletano et al., 2011; Saburi et al., 2012; Sharma and McNeill, 2013.

claim: ChIP-seq identified 1300 potential direct targets of Atro including engrailed, and components of the Dpp and Notch signaling pathways.
source: ChIP-seq identified 1300 potential direct targets of Atro including engrailed, and components of the Dpp and Notch signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by experimental ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atro regulates Dpp and Notch signaling in larval imaginal discs, at least partially via regulation of thickveins and fringe.
source: We show that Atro regulates Dpp and Notch signaling in larval imaginal discs, at least partially via regulation of thickveins and fringe.
evidence: Supported by experimental data including in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atro interacts with the Drosophila GAGA Factor, Trithorax-like (Trl), and they bind to the same loci simultaneously.
source: In addition, bioinformatics analyses, sequential ChIP and coimmunoprecipitation experiments reveal that Atro interacts with the Drosophila GAGA Factor, Trithorax-like (Trl), and they bind to the same loci simultaneously.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-re-ChIP and coimmunoprecipitation experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atro is required to modulate the transcription activation by Trl in larval imaginal discs.
source: Phenotypic analyses of Trl and Atro clones suggest that Atro is required to modulate the transcription activation by Trl in larval imaginal discs.
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analyses of mutant clones presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atro is a major Trl cofactor that functions to moderate developmental gene transcription.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that Atro is a major Trl cofactor that functions to moderate developmental gene transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the combined ChIP-seq, ChIP-re-ChIP, and phenotypic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A polyglutamine expansion in ATN1 is responsible for dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA).
source: A polyglutamine expansion in ATN1 is responsible for dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) a progressive disorder of ataxia, myoclonus, epilepsy, intellectual deterioration and dementia (Koide et al., 1994; Nagafuchi et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koide et al., 1994 and Nagafuchi et al., 1994.

claim: Expression of polyglutamine expansion Atro in Drosophila leads to neurodegeneration.
source: Drosophila has only one Atrophin (Atro) gene, and expression of polyglutamine expansion Atro also lead to neurodegeneration (Napoletano et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Napoletano et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of Atro results in defects in planar polarity, segmentation, and eye, wing and leg developmental defects.
source: Loss of Atro results in defects in planar polarity, segmentation, and eye, wing and leg developmental defects (Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2002; Fanto et al., 2003; Charroux et al., 2006; Napoletano et al., 2011; Saburi et al., 2012; Sharma and McNeill, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Atro is required for proper expression of en in the embryo and represses the gap genes Krüppel and knirps.
source: Atro is required for proper expression of en in the embryo and represses the gap genes Krüppel and knirps (Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2002; Haecker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2002; Haecker et al., 2007.

claim: Atro affects epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), Decapentaplegic (Dpp) and Hedgehog signaling.
source: Atro also affects epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), Decapentaplegic (Dpp) and Hedgehog signaling (Erkner et al., 2002; Charroux et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkner et al., 2002; Charroux et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Only three direct Atro targets have been defined: knirps, fat and dpp.
source: Despite regulating many pathways and processes, only three direct Atro targets have been defined (knirps, fat and dpp) (Wang et al., 2006; Napoletano et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006; Napoletano et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Atro physically interacts with histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) through its SANT domain.
source: Atro physically interacts with histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) and the histone methyltransferase, G9a, through its SANT and ELM2 domains, respectively (Figure 1A) (Wang et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: Atro physically interacts with the histone methyltransferase G9a through its ELM2 domain.
source: Atro physically interacts with histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) and the histone methyltransferase, G9a, through its SANT and ELM2 domains, respectively (Figure 1A) (Wang et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: Atro interacts with the co-repressor Scribbler (also called Brakeless).
source: Atro also interacts with other cofactors such as the co-repressor, Scribbler (also called Brakeless) (Wang et al., 2006; Haecker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006; Haecker et al., 2007.

claim: Atro does not have a DNA-binding sequence and has been shown to interact with DNA via interactions with nuclear receptors.
source: Atro does not have a DNA-binding sequence and has been shown to interact with DNA via interactions with nuclear receptors (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2006.

claim: Trl is an essential transcription factor that directly binds to GA repeats.
source: Trl is an essential transcription factor that directly binds to GA repeats (Biggin and Tjian, 1988; Soeller et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biggin and Tjian, 1988; Soeller et al., 1988.

claim: Trl regulates the segment polarity gene engrailed (en).
source: Trl regulates many developmentally important genes including the segment polarity gene, engrailed (en) (Farkas et al., 1994; Bejarano and Busturia, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Farkas et al., 1994; Bejarano and Busturia, 2004.

claim: Trl can interact with other transcription factors (e.g. Yorkie, Tramtrack) to regulate transcriptional targets in patterning and growth control.
source: Trl can interact with other transcription factors (e.g. Yorkie, Tramtrack) to regulate transcriptional targets in patterning and growth control (Pagans et al., 2002; Oh et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pagans et al., 2002; Oh et al., 2013.

claim: The majority of Atro peaks are located in actively transcribed genes, often close to the promoters or in introns.
source: We further mapped the 1377 Atro peaks relative to gene features and gene expression, which showed that the majority of peaks are located in actively transcribed genes, often close to the promoters or in introns (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Class 2 Atro peaks are strongly enriched with Polycomb factors.
source: We noticed that Class 2 (blue, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) peaks are strongly enriched with Polycomb factors, indicating a potential connection between Atro and Polycomb factors.
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There are two strong Atro peaks in the en promoter within 2.4 kb upstream of the transcription start site.
source: There are two strong Atro peaks in the en promoter (Figure 1E, within 2.4 kb upstream of the transcription start site [Kassis et al., 1992]).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Kassis et al., 1992.

claim: Atro35 clones have increased En levels in antennal, wing and leg imaginal discs.
source: We found Atro35 clones have increased En levels in antennal, wing and leg imaginal discs (Figure 2A,B, and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Atro35 clones only show increased En levels in clones located in the posterior compartment, where En is endogenously expressed.
source: Interestingly, Atro35 clones only show increased En levels in clones located in the posterior compartment, where En is endogenously expressed (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Atro negatively modulates En expression levels to maintain moderate expression in imaginal discs.
source: These data suggest that Atro negatively modulates En expression levels to maintain moderate expression in imaginal discs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atro35 clones have increased En levels in the posterior compartment but cannot induce ectopic En in the anterior compartment.

claim: Several Atro peaks occur in putative regulatory regions of several Dpp signaling pathway components (e.g. thickveins, Daughters against dpp and schnurri).
source: Interestingly, our ChIP-seq data show that several Atro peaks occur in putative regulatory regions of several Dpp signaling pathway components (e.g. thickveins, Daughters against dpp and schnurri, Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1), suggesting Atro regulates Dpp signaling by directly regulating the expression of Dpp signaling pathway components.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Atro35 clones show upregulation of the tkv-LacZ reporter in the wing.
source: Thickveins (Tkv) is a critical Dpp receptor, and Atro35 clones show upregulation of the tkv-LacZ reporter in the wing (Wehn and Campbell, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wehn and Campbell, 2006.

claim: tkv expression is increased if Atro is knocked down.
source: To confirm that Atro represses tkv expression, tkv transcript levels were assessed in Atro knocked down wing discs using in situ hybridization. Indeed, tkv expression is increased if Atro is knocked down (Figure 3B), confirming Atro represses tkv expression in the wing.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Atro35 clones that cross the endogenous pMad regions have increased pMad levels along the interior border of the clone that is closest to the middle of the disc.
source: Atro35 clones that are found in the endogenous pMad regions have increased pMad levels along the interior border of the clones that is closest to the centre of the discs, where the endogenous Dpp source is located (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Atro35 clones have increased Optomotor blind (Omb) expression, indicating increased Dpp signaling in the clones.
source: Atro35 clones also have increased Optomotor blind (Omb, a downstream target of Dpp signaling) expression (data not shown), indicating increased Dpp signaling in the clones (Grimm and Pflugfelder, 1996).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Grimm and Pflugfelder, 1996.

claim: Atro35 clones far from the Dpp source do not induce ectopic Mad phosphorylation.
source: However, Atro35 clones far from the Dpp source do not induce ectopic Mad phosphorylation, suggesting Dpp levels are not increased in Atro35 clones (Figure 3D, arrow heads).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Atro35 clones in the anterior or posterior compartments do not cause ectopic Dpp expression.
source: Consistent with this, Atro35 clones in the anterior or posterior compartments do not cause ectopic Dpp expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Atro directly regulates tkv expression and thereby Dpp signaling.
source: Our data indicate that Atro directly regulates tkv expression and thereby Dpp signaling.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data showing Atro binding at tkv locus and phenotypic data showing increased pMad in Atro35 clones.

claim: Atro binds the putative regulatory regions of several Notch signaling components (mastermind, Delta, neuralized and fringe).
source: Atro ChIP data also revealed that Atro binds the putative regulatory regions of several Notch signaling components (mastermind (mam), Delta (Dl), neuralized (neur) and fringe (fng) (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that Atro may regulate Notch signaling.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Atro genetically interacts with Notch.
source: Thus, Atro genetically interacts with N, suggesting Atro may play a role in N signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic interaction data showing enhanced wing notching in transheterozygous mutants.

claim: Atro35 clones cause the Notch signaling reporter (NRE-GFP) to express in a diffused pattern.
source: Atro35 clones that cross the wing margin disrupt the expression pattern of the NRE-GFP reporter (Figure 4C), resulting in diffuse expression of the NRE-GFP reporter.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Large Atro35 clones cause an autonomous loss of wing margin marker Cut as well as ectopic Cut expression on the posterior side of the clone.
source: In addition, Atro35 clones that cross the wing margin cause a loss of wing margin markers (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). In some cases, Atro35 clones induce ectopic Ct expression just outside of the posterior clonal border (Figure 4D, arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Atro35 clones do not affect Cut expression in the antennal discs.
source: In contrast to the wing, Atro35 clones do not affect Ct expression in the antennal discs, where a requirement of N signaling for Ct expression has not been shown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atro35 clones have extra Sens positive cells clustered together in groups of two to three cells, resembling the number and shape of the R2/5/8 equivalence group.
source: Atro35 clones have extra Sens positive cells (Figure 4E), clustered together in groups of two to three cells, resembling the number and shape of the R2/5/8 equivalence group.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There is one cell that has more Sens staining than the rest within each Sens-positive cell cluster in Atro35 clones.
source: However, we noticed that there is one cell that has more Sens staining than the rest within each Sens-positive cell cluster (Figure 4E, arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Atro35 clones do not have an excess of cells marked with a late R8 marker, Bride of sevenless (Boss).
source: Although Atro35 clones can induce extra Sens-positive cells, these clones do not have an excess of cells marked with a late R8 marker, Bride of sevenless (Boss) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Atro35 clones lose R7 and cone cell markers.
source: We found that Atro35 clones also lose R7 and cone cell markers (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Atro35 clones have reduced Emc protein levels anterior to the morphogenetic furrow.
source: Indeed, Atro35 clones have reduced Emc protein levels anterior to the morphogenetic furrow (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The top motif discovered in Atro ChIP-seq data is a GA repeat, the binding motif of Trithorax-like (Trl).
source: Therefore, we performed de novo motif analysis of our ChIP-seq data using MEME-ChIP (Bailey et al., 2009) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The top motif discovered is a GA repeat, the binding motif of Trithorax-like (Trl, Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by MEME-ChIP analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Trl binding motif is enriched within Atro ChIP peak summits.
source: The Trl binding motif is enriched within Atro ChIP peak summits, indicating strongest Atro binding.
evidence: Inferred from the MEME-ChIP analysis showing Trl motif as the top hit.

claim: Other enriched motifs in Atro ChIP-seq data include Twin of eyeless (Toy) and Mad.
source: Other enriched motifs include Twin of eyeless (Toy) and Mad (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by MEME-ChIP analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The strongest overlap of Atro ChIP-seq data with other transcription factors was found with Trl.
source: In this analysis, several factors, including Trl, CBP (Nejire), the replication proteins Orc2 and MCM, Yorkie (Yki) and Polycomb proteins, showed increased overlap with increasing Atro binding (Figure 5B). Interestingly, the strongest overlap was found with Trl, confirming the MEME-ChIP analysis (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 1123 out of 1377 Atro peaks overlap with Trl ChIP peaks.
source: We further compared our list of Atro peaks with the published Trl ChIP-seq data (Fuda et al., 2015) and found striking overlap between the two data sets (1123/1377 Atro peaks overlap with Trl ChIP, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5C and citation to Fuda et al., 2015.

claim: Endogenous Trl can be coimmunoprecipitated with endogenous Atro after pretreatment with micrococcal nuclease.
source: Although we did not detect an interaction using standard coIP conditions, pretreating lysates with micrococcal nuclease allowed us to coimmunoprecipitate endogenous Trl with endogenous Atro (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D (note: the text refers to Figure 5D but the actual figure is Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Atro-Trl ChIP-re-ChIP enriches for loci with both Atro and Trl peaks.
source: qPCR show that Atro-Trl ChIP-re-ChIP enriches for the locus with both Atro and Trl peaks, while it does not enrich for a locus with only Atro peak (enrichment is nearly equal to Atro-IgG ChIP-re-ChIP-negative control) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-re-ChIP qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Atro and Trl co-occupy all the tested loci with both Atro and Trl peaks.
source: Additional experiments showed that Atro and Trl co-occupy all the tested loci with both Atro and Trl peaks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-re-ChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knock down of Trl leads to reduced abundance of Atro proteins.
source: Unfortunately, we could not directly test if Atro association with DNA requires Trl in cells, as knock down of Trl also leads to reduced abundance of Atro proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Atro and Trl bind to the same loci and to one another, forming a complex on chromatin to regulate transcription.
source: These findings indicate that Atro and Trl bind to the same loci and to one another, forming a complex on chromatin to regulate transcription.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-re-ChIP and coimmunoprecipitation data.

claim: There are strong overlaps of Atro and Trl ChIP-seq peaks at the en locus.
source: Both ChIP-seq and ChIP-re-ChIP data show that Atro and Trl bind to the same loci simultaneously. Interestingly, there are strong overlaps of Atro and Trl ChIP-seq peaks at the en locus (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TrlR85 clones have reduced En expression.
source: In contrast to Atro35 clones, TrlR85 clones have reduced En expression (Figure 6D), indicating that Trl is required for the positive regulation of En expression in larval discs.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Trl is required for the positive regulation of En expression in larval discs.
source: In contrast to Atro35 clones, TrlR85 clones have reduced En expression (Figure 6D), indicating that Trl is required for the positive regulation of En expression in larval discs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrlR85 clones have reduced En expression.

claim: Atro and Trl bind to the same region of the tkv locus.
source: Atro and Trl ChIP-seq data also indicate that Atro and Trl bind to the same region of the tkv locus (Figure 6E), suggesting that Trl regulates tkv expression with Atro.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: TrlR85 clones have reduced pMad levels.
source: In contrast to Atro35 clones, TrlR85 clones have reduced pMad levels (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The reduced pMad in TrlR85 clones is caused by a downregulation of tkv expression.
source: Thus, the simplest model to explain our data is that the reduced pMad in TrlR85 clones is caused by a downregulation of tkv expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrlR85 clones have reduced pMad levels and the absence of Trl or Atro peaks within 20 kb of the mad locus.

claim: Trl is required for tkv expression, while Atro is required for repression of tkv.
source: Therefore, similar to Atro and Trl's regulation of en, Trl is required for tkv expression, while Atro is required for repression of tkv.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotypic data showing opposite effects of Atro35 and TrlR85 clones on tkv expression and pMad levels.

claim: Atro binds to DNA via Trl, either directly or indirectly via some unknown cofactors, and Atro modulates transcriptional activation by Trl.
source: Atro does not bind to DNA directly, while Trl has a DNA binding domain (Biggin and Tjian, 1988). Thus, our results suggest a model in which Atro binds to DNA via Trl, either directly or indirectly via someunknown cofactors, and Atro modulates transcriptional activation by Trl.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atro does not bind DNA directly, Trl has a DNA binding domain, and they bind to the same loci simultaneously.

claim: Trl binding leads to open chromatin to allow transcription, and Atro binding negatively modulates Trl's activity.
source: To explain these phenotypes, we propose a model in which Trl binding leads to open chromatin to allow transcription, and Atro binding, either by directly interacting with Trl or through some unknown factors, negatively modulates Trl's activity (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined data from the manuscript.

claim: Atro binds to Histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) and a histone methyltransferase (G9a) to close chromatin and repress transcription.
source: Atro binds to Histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) and a histone methyltransferase (G9a) to close chromatin and repress transcription (Wang et al., 2006, 2008), suggesting a mechanisms by which Atro is able to counteract Trl.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2006, 2008.

claim: Atro- and Trl-binding sites at the en, tkv and fng loci overlap with HDAC1-binding sites.
source: Indeed, Atro- and Trl-binding sites at the en, tkv and fng loci overlap with HDAC1-binding sites (from modENCODE, RPD3-Q3451) (Celniker et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by comparison with modENCODE data and citation to Celniker et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of Trl leads to loss of expression of en and tkv where they are normally expressed.
source: Thus, loss of Trl leads to loss of expression of en and tkv where they are normally expressed.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrlR85 clones have reduced En expression and reduced pMad levels.

claim: In the absence of Atro, Trl's activity is no longer negatively modulated, and expression of target genes such as en and tkv are increased.
source: In the absence of Atro, Trl's activity is no longer negatively modulated, and expression of target genes such as en and tkv are increased.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atro35 clones have increased En levels and increased tkv expression.

claim: In regions where en and tkv are not endogenously expressed, loss of Atro cannot induce ectopic expression as Atro's function is to negatively modulate the transcription of its target genes.
source: However, in regions where en and tkv are not endogenously expressed, loss of Atro cannot induce ectopic expression as Atro's function is to negatively modulate the transcription of its target genes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atro35 clones cannot induce ectopic En expression in the anterior compartment.

claim: Trl is enriched at paused promoters and is involved in transcription pausing.
source: Interestingly, Trl is enriched at paused promoters and is involved in transcription pausing (Lee et al., 2008; Fuda et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2008; Fuda et al., 2015.

claim: Trl recruits the negative elongation factor NELF to paused genes.
source: Trl recruits the negative elongation factor NELF to paused genes (Li et al., 2013), but the precise mechanism of how Trl affects pausing is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: The pausing index increase is even higher for genes bound by both Atro and Trl than genes bound only by Trl.
source: This increase of pausing index is even higher than genes bound only by Trl (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by pausing index analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Atro may be involved in transcriptional pausing with Trl.
source: These data suggest that Atro may be involved in transcriptional pausing with Trl.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that genes bound by both Atro and Trl have higher pausing index.

claim: There are some Atro-binding sites that are not co-occupied by Trl.
source: We note that there are some Atro-binding sites that are not co-occupied by Trl.
evidence: Inferred from the overlap analysis showing 254 Atro peaks do not overlap with Trl peaks.

claim: Atro peaks that do not overlap with Trl peaks are slightly weaker than the ones that do.
source: Visual inspection reveals strong Atro peaks that do overlap with Trl (Figure 6A); however, on a genome-wide basis, Atro peaks that do not overlap with Trl peaks are slightly weaker than the ones that do, as judged from the MACS2 derived significance (-log(p-value)) and fold enrichment values (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Atro maternal mutants have missing, malformed and/or expanded En stripes.
source: Atro maternal mutants have missing, malformed and/or expanded En stripes (Zhang et al., 2002), while in discs Atro modulates En expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: During early embryogenesis, Pair-rule genes are required to first establish en expression.
source: During early embryogenesis, Pair-rule genes are required to first establish en expression (DiNardo et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to DiNardo et al., 1988.

claim: Atro is required for the proper expression of Pair-rule genes such as fushi tarazu and even-skipped.
source: Atro is also required for the proper expression of Pair-rule genes such as fushi tarazu and even-skipped (Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: From late embryogenesis on, En expression no longer requires Pair-rule genes but depends on Polycomb group genes and unidentified activators.
source: However, from late embryogenesis on, En expression no longer requires Pair-rule genes but depends on Polycomb group genes and unidentified activators (Moazed and O'Farrell, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moazed and O'Farrell, 1992.

claim: Trl and Atro are required for regulation of En expression from late embryogenesis through larval development.
source: We observed reduced En expression in Trl clones in antennal and wing imaginal discs, while Atro disc clones have increased expression. These results suggest that Trl and Atro are required for regulation of En expression from late embryogenesis through larval development.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotypic data showing opposite effects of Trl and Atro clones on En expression in imaginal discs.

claim: Expressing higher than normal levels of En in the posterior compartment leads to lethality and anterior-posterior patterning defects of the posterior wing.
source: Intriguingly, expressing higher than normal levels of En in the posterior compartment leads to lethality and anterior-posterior patterning defects of the posterior wing, suggesting that moderating En levels is required for normal development, and high levels could be toxic (Guillén et al., 1995; Tabata et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guillén et al., 1995; Tabata et al., 1995.

claim: Moderating En levels is required for normal development, and high levels could be toxic.
source: Intriguingly, expressing higher than normal levels of En in the posterior compartment leads to lethality and anterior-posterior patterning defects of the posterior wing, suggesting that moderating En levels is required for normal development, and high levels could be toxic (Guillén et al., 1995; Tabata et al., 1995).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that overexpression of En leads to lethality and patterning defects.

claim: Atro35 clones can lead to ectopic dpp-LacZ expression.
source: Although Atro35 clones can lead to ectopic dpp-LacZ expression (Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2013), we did not see increased Dpp in Atro35 wing clones.
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkner et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Atro regulates Dpp signaling in the wing primarily by regulating tkv transcription.
source: Thus, we suggest that Atro regulates Dpp signaling in the wing primarily by regulating tkv transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atro35 clones increase pMad in a pattern consistent with increased Tkv levels but do not increase Dpp expression.

claim: Atro knockdown results in upregulation of fng transcripts in larval wings.
source: Atro knockdown results in upregulation of fng transcripts in larval wings.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: patched-Gal4-driven overexpression of fng leads to an autonomous loss of wing margin marker expression as well as ectopic expression of wing margin marker on the posterior border of the Fng overexpressing region.
source: Interestingly, patched-Gal4-driven overexpression of fng leads to an autonomous loss of wing margin marker expression as well as ectopic expression of wing margin marker on the posterior border of the Fng overexpressing region (Panin et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Panin et al., 1997.

claim: All Atro35 clones that cross the wing margin cause an autonomous loss of wing margin markers and large Atro35 clones can induce some ectopic wing margin marker expression on the posterior edge of the clone, mimicking patched-Gal4-driven Fng overexpression.
source: All Atro35 clones that cross the wing margin cause an autonomous loss of wing margin markers and large Atro35 clones can induce some ectopic wing margin marker expression on the posterior edge of the clone, mimicking patched-Gal4-driven Fng overexpression.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fng is crucial for N signaling at the margin.
source: Interestingly, Fng is crucial for N signaling at the margin (de Celis and Bray, 1997; Panin et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Celis and Bray, 1997; Panin et al., 1997.

claim: Atro represses fng expression.
source: Thus, Atro represses fng expression, and loss of Atro and patched-Gal4-driven overexpression of Fng have similar N-related phenotype in the wing.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Atro knockdown increases fng transcripts and Atro35 clones have similar phenotypes to Fng overexpression.

claim: Loss of Atro and patched-Gal4-driven overexpression of Fng have similar N-related phenotype in the wing.
source: Thus, Atro represses fng expression, and loss of Atro and patched-Gal4-driven overexpression of Fng have similar N-related phenotype in the wing.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between Atro35 clones and Fng overexpression.

claim: Significant overlap of Atro ChIP-seq data with ChIP data sets of Yorkie (Yki) was observed.
source: While the strongest overlap in our ChIP-seq peaks was seen between Atro and Trl, we also observed significant overlap of our Atro ChIP-seq data with ChIP data sets of Yorkie (Yki), the key transcriptional co-activator of the Hippo pathway (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neurodegeneration by Atro has been shown to be mediated in part by Yki and the Hippo pathway.
source: Significantly, neurodegeneration by Atro has been shown to be mediated in part by Yki and the Hippo pathway (Napoletano et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Napoletano et al., 2011.

claim: Atro interactions with Yki may feed back into growth and patterning regulation by Fat cadherins.
source: Thererfore, our finding that Yki and Atro are found at the same loci suggests a direct mechanism by which Atro may impact neurodegeneration, and suggests that Atro interactions with Yki may feed back into growth and patterning regulation by Fat cadherins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the overlap of Atro and Yki ChIP-seq data and known interactions.

claim: Atro preferentially binds to Trl binding sites.
source: Our genome-wide ChIP-seq and phenotypic analyses reveal many novel direct targets of Atro, and showed that Engrailed, Notch and Dpp signaling are directly regulated by Atro. Our analyses indicate that Atro preferentially binds to Trl binding sites.
evidence: Inferred from the strong overlap between Atro and Trl ChIP-seq data.

claim: The fraction of paused genes is significantly more correlated with sites that bind both Atro and Trl, than just Trl alone.
source: Interestingly, the fraction of paused genes is significantly more correlated with sites that bind both Atro and Trl, than just Trl alone, suggesting Atro may have a function in the regulation of pausing.
evidence: Supported by pausing index analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Atro is a critical component of developmental signaling and is an important general modulator of transcription activation by Trl.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that Atro is a critical component of developmental signaling and is an important general modulator of transcription activation by Trl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the manuscript.
